## Stationary does not always mean turning {#gac3-example-1-15 .gac-lesson }

```{=html}
<p class="gac3-example-label">Example 1.15</p>
<p class="gac3-source">Classify the labelled points on the curve below.</p>
<img class="gac3-source-graph gac3-classify-graph" src="../media/example-1-15.svg" alt="Original booklet curve with points A to F. A and F are troughs, C is a peak, and E has a horizontal tangent without turning.">
<p class="booklet-cue">Example 1.15 · Booklet p. 20</p>
```

::: notes
3 minutes. Introduce the three types of smooth stationary point, then classify the supplied graph. A and F: local minimum turning points. C: local maximum turning point. E: horizontal/stationary point of inflection. B and D: non-stationary points of inflection as drawn; their tangents are respectively positive and negative. Briefly explain that an inflection changes the way the curve bends, and need not have a horizontal tangent. Formal concavity and tests for inflection are next lesson.

Local refers to nearby values, not the greatest or least value over the whole domain. Horizontal gradient alone does not distinguish a maximum, minimum or horizontal inflection. The classification here concerns the smooth stationary points in the supplied examples; extrema can also occur at corners/endpoints, considered later. Do not infer an exact formula from this schematic source graph.
:::
